textbookText: Figure 8.4.17 Artery in frog Histologically, wall of artery consists of outermost fibrous layer of collagen (tunica adventitia), middle thick muscular layer and innermost layer of squamous epithelial cells (endothelium). Muscular layer is well developed in arteries.

Figure 8.4.18 T.S. of artery 2. Capillaries: Capillaries are fine thread like network of blood vessels extending all body tissues. Their wall is extremely thin which i.e made up of single layer of squamous epithelial cell called endothelium. There is no muscular and fibrous layer in the capillary wall. Capillaries are found abundantly in muscles and glands. Because of their thin wall exchange of nutrients, gases, hormones, waste occurs in between blood and tissues under pressure. Capillaries form a network around organ or tissue between the arterioles and venules. But in some organs like liver, spleen and red bone marrow, irregular blood spaces called sinusoids replace blood capillaries.

3. Veins: Veins are thin walled, inelastic blood vessels having wide lumen. They transport blood from different parts of the body to the heart. Comparatively, there is less pressure of blood on the wall of veins so they have valves at frequent intervals. Valves in the veins check reverse flow of blood. Veins are superficially situated in the body. Generally, veins transport deoxygenated blood but in the case of frog, they carry mixed blood. These vessels collapse after cut or death easily because of their feebly developed muscular wall. Veins divides into fine branches called venules.

Histologically, wall of vein consists of outermost fibrous layer of collagen (tunica adventitia), middle thin muscular layer and innermost layer of squamous epithelial cells (endothelium). Muscular layer is poorly developed in veins.

Blood is a liquid connective tissue composed of different type of blood cells suspended freely in a clear liquid called plasma. It keeps circulating in closed tubes called blood vessels throughout the body. Generally, Blood pH is 7. Blood consists of mainly 2 parts: Plasma and Blood corpuscles.

1. Plasma Plasma is non-living, clear, pale yellow, slightly alkaline watery portion comprising about 55% of the blood. Dissolved substances in the plasma are nutrients, mineral salts, urea, hormones, proteins and other soluble substances. Major proteins found in plasma are serum albumin, serum globulin, fibrinogen and Heparin. Serum albumen has role in maintaining osmotic pressure and serum globulin forms enzymes and antibodies. Fibrinogen has role in clotting of blood in wound and injuries and heparin is an anticoagulant which prevents blood clotting in blood vessels.

Functions of plasma: i. Plasma transports nutrients, hormones, oxygen and metabolic wastes like urea carbon dioxide to the respective parts of the body. ii. Plasma proteins perform various functions such as maintaining blood osmotic pressure; neutralize damaged body protein, toxin and engulf germs. iii. Some plasma proten like fibrinogen helps in clotting of blood during cut etc.

2. Blood cells or blood corpuscles a. Red blood cells or Erythrocytes Red coloured cells (RBCs) are numerous (about 2.5-4 million per cubic mm of blood), oval, flattened, nucleated, and biconvex in shape. RBCs have respiratory pigment called haemoglobin. Hemoglobin transports oxygen to the tissues in the form of oxy-haemoglobin and also imparts red colour to the blood. They are formed in liver and speen and destroyed in the same organs. In frog, their life span is about 100 days.

Functions of RBC i. RBCs transport oxygen from lungs to tissues (in oxyhaemoglobin form) and carbon dioxide (in carbamino form) from tissues to lungs. ii. RBCs also have role in maintaining pH of blood. iii. They maintain viscosity of blood.

b. White blood cells or Leucocytes White blood cells are colourless and without haemoglobin, fewer (5000-7000 per cubic mm), nucleated and amoeboid shaped. They are formed in liver, yellow bone marrow and spleen in frog. Life span is about 20 days. Their number increases during infection. They engulf dead cell and bacteria through phagocytosis and also called phagocytes. Because of their changeable shape, they squeeze through capillary wall and show diapedesis.
Leucocytes are polymorphic i.e. found in different form. On the basis of presence or absence of granules in cytoplasm, they are granulocytes and agranulocytes.
a. Granulocytes: i. They are irregular shaped cells and filled with granular cytoplasm with specific staining property. ii. Nucleus is variable shaped and strongly lobulated.
iii. Granulocytes are more numerous (about 70% of total leucocytes) and produced in red bone marrow.
